Orders for Returns
2.	It has been reported that two out of 50 samples of waxes examined contain dibenzanthracene in amounts of the order of one part per million and one half part per billion of the wax. speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Transport of which I have sent him notice. Mail for the coast communities is being forwarded either by air or by the services I have mentioned. Passengers will have to rely on the many air services available on the British Columbia coast, because there is no alternative steamship company with vessels available and capable of performing the required services.
The services I have described will not be as convenient as those normally given by Northland Navigation Company, but the communities served will receive the basic supplies necessary for their existence.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. In doing so, of course, I appreciate the friendly attitude the minister has taken toward me personally, but I rise not only on a point of order but on a question of privilege that affects this house.
The minister in giving his reply said he would be pleased to give an extended reply as a favour to the hon. member for Essex East who, along with two other hon. members, he said, had shown some interest in this matter. A minister's answer is not given to an hon. member as a matter of favour but as a matter of right. This is the House of Commons, and when questions are put to ministers of the crown, to those who sit on the treasury benches, answers made by them are not made out of their goodness and kindness of heart and friendship toward one member; they must be made under our constitutional practice as a matter of duty involving the recognition of the rights of parliament itself. While I appreciate the friendly attitude of the minister, I should remind him that he is a member of a government whose party and whose leader has insisted that the rights of parliament must at all times be observed.

speechtext: The house resumed, from Tuesday, July 14, consideration of the motion of Mr. Fleming (Eglinton) for the second reading of Bill No. C-72, to provide for the payment of additional grants to the province of Newfoundland.

subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE ADDITIONAL GRANTS TO NEWFOUNDLAND
speechtext:
Last evening Mr. Speaker, when the house rose at ten o'clock I had said that Bill No. C-72 was a complete and definite denial of the constitutional rights of Newfoundland. I had made some remarks in reference to the table placed on Hansard by the Minister of Finance and to be found at page 5901, and had suggested to him that similar information for other Atlantic provinces be provided during the committee stage; and that a table showing the amount of money collected from the province of Newfoundland be provided at that time also.
May I go along, Mr. Speaker, and say that while any statement with regard to the amount of money paid to the province of Newfoundland by the federal government and any statement with regard to the amount of money collected by the federal government from Newfoundland are extremely important, nevertheless there are other considerations. I am sure this house will not fail to appreciate the important advantages that were brought to Canada in 1949, the date of union. There was a territory of over 150,000 square miles added to Canada, with a population of over 400,000, to which must be added to the industrial potential of the province itself. Forest products is one of the major industries in Canada if not the major industry. Production in that industry was increased by 10 per cent with the union of Newfoundland with Canada. Added to these we have the production of our fisheries and our mines, and also the potential water power which exists at bay d'Espoir and at Grand Falls, Labrador. Certainly, too, we must not forget the improved defensive position which was created by the addition of Newfoundland to Canada.
Before confederation Newfoundland bought from the Canadian mainland approximately
[Mr. Pickersgill.l
$50 million worth of imports. Today imports to Newfoundland from the mainland of Canada are five times that amount. Here we have a province which, if it were not a province of Canada and still imported the same amount that it does now, would as far as imports are concerned be Canada's third best customer. Here we have a market where nearly everything that is produced has to be sold outside the confines of Canada, and nearly everything that is used is imported from the mainland of Canada.
I do not think there is any better statement I could make to describe this situation than that made by the Newfoundland board of trade to the Prime Minister under date of April 13, 1959. On page 2 of that letter, in the first paragraph, this statement is made:
Because the economy of Newfoundland depends so largely upon the primary industries of fishing, mining and forestry, and we are without secondary manufacturing industries, our income "leaks out" of the island directly and at once to the central manufacturing areas of Ontario and Quebec, from which we draw our supplies. In view of this, an expenditure in Newfoundland is almost as successful in stimulating the economy of Ontario and Quebec as is a direct expenditure in either of these provinces. Because of heavy purchases by Newfoundland from the rest of Canada, and since other parts of Canada purchase little from Newfoundland, there is a serious "balance of payments" problem between Newfoundland and the rest of Canada. The federal government alone can offset this income "leakage" by transfer payments of various kinds.
I would like to go further, Mr. Speaker, and say that I disagree completely with the way the government has handled this bill. First of all we had the report of the McNair commission upon which the Prime Minister made some statements, if my memory serves me correctly, last August, almost a year ago. This bill is brought in now, almost a year later, in the dying days of the session. It is my opinion that this bill deserves a more important place in the legislative program of this particular session.
The statement of the Prime Minister on March 25 certainly allayed no fears in the minds of the people of Newfoundland. Then the Minister of Justice went down to Newfoundland and made his speech on Thursday, May 14. There is no need to add any further comments about that, but I would refer to an editorial in the St. John's Daily News of Friday, May 15 with reference to the statements made by the Minister of Justice. The-editorial begins:
Mr. Fulton, the federal Minister of Justice, said; in his address to the Newfoundland board of trade that it was time to put the record straight in respect of Newfoundland's relations with the government of Canada. Mr. Fulton spoke for an hour. The record was still unstraightened after he had. finished.

He seemed to have two main objectives. One was to assure us of his government's good will and good intentions. The other was to convince us that the Prime Minister's decision on term 29 was good for Newfoundland. He has failed.
Then, Mr. Speaker, the editorial goes on:
He has copied Mr. Diefenbaker's attempt to convince us of Canada's generosity by setting out the allocations we have received from Ottawa as if they were special to this province-
He was plausible. He was pleasant. He was possibly good-intentioned. But he was completely unconvincing, completely unfamiliar with our case under the terms of union, and completely a failure as a peacemaker. We had hoped for better results from his visit.
I say again, Mr. Speaker, that I regret that this matter has been handled in the way it has. I thought yesterday when the Prime Minister was speaking that this particular topic deserved a little more serious consideration than was given to it. When the Prime Minister defends an issue as he did yesterday he does so for one of two reasons. Either there is political kudos to be obtained, or there is something to be defended. I was interested, too, in the statement made by the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Browne); and while he certainly obtained the applause of this house last evening I suggest to you that he would not obtain the applause of Newfoundlanders.
I have already made reference to the Atlantic grants, and I am not going to go further into them now. Neither am I going to outline, because it has been outlined by other hon. members, the real need for term 29. Let me finish by saying this. Newfoundlanders will ask the question, by virtue of what logic can a nebulous pledge be accepted by them when a firm contractual obligation under the British North America Act has not been honoured by this government?

I suggest that this is good legislation. It is the best legislation that could possibly come out of such a nebulous and meaningless clause as term 29 in the drafting of which no doubt my friend the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate had some hand. Here again we have had some extraordinary sophistry on the part of hon. members opposite. The royal commission has made its recommendations. What effect have these? Here I need do no more than cite the words of the Leader of the Opposition yesterday as recorded at page 5989 of Hansard of July 14. I put the following question to him:
Does the Leader of the Opposition contend that the recommendations of the royal commission are binding on the federal government?
His answer was:
Of course not. I said yesterday that no recommendation of a royal commission is legally binding on any government.
The Leader of the Opposition is quite correct. There was no binding effect so far as the recommendations of the royal commission are concerned. It is perfectly clear. It remained, then, in the light of the terms of article 29, in the light of this authoritative interpretation by Mr. St. Laurent, a matter for decision by parliament. There is nothing 

said there about further negociation. There is nothing said there about entering into a new agreement. No, not at all; article 29 simply leaves it to parliament, as Mr. St. Laurent has said, and it is not left with any suggestion of any binding effect that those recommendations might have upon parliament. There is no such binding effect so there is no obligation up to that point. These recommendations are not binding on the federal government nor are they binding on the federal parliament. We do not say they are binding on Newfoundland either.
Newfoundland through its premier is entitled to approve them or criticize them as he chooses. No one will deny him that right. Nor is there anything to prevent him asking for more, as he did when we met with him in January last. That is his right. But there is no right-and here I wish to be very clear and emphatic in regard to this alleged obligation-there is no right, contractual or constitutional, on the part of anyone in this country to the implementation of the recommendations of this royal commission in whole or in part.
Hon. members opposite in going on talking about an obligation are simply doing so in the face of clear and uncontestable facts. A fair test of the effect of this constitutional provision in article 29 is to test it under other circumstances for its meaning. Had circumstances been different, it is perfectly clear that under the terms of article 29 the royal commission might-as I say, had circumstances warranted it-have recommended larger or smaller payments, or no payments, or payments for a year, or six months, or two years, or for any period the royal commission might have chosen. It was not left for further negotiation of a new agreement. Article 29 and the other terms of union were final in their terms, Mr. Speaker. What was required at that point, Mr. St. Laurent makes crystal clear, was a decision by the Canadian parliament. If hon. members opposite today do not like that procedure they can take the responsibility upon themselves, because it was they who drew article 29.

An assessment in detail of each claim is not possible as the claims are for the most part based upon broad and general considerations of fairness and equity having regard to the treatment enjoyed by other provinces under the same headings and to the economic disadvantages to which the maritime provinces are peculiarly subject owing to their isolated geographic position in relation to the central and western parts of Canada toward which the trend of Canadian development has continuously and increasingly set ever since the establishment of the dominion. Such claims are by their nature not susceptible of detailed appraisal by any process of mathematical calculation as the

Grants to Newfoundland
basis for accurate comparison is wanting on account of the diversity of conditions and circumstances of development of the several provinces.
It was then stated:
As an assessment in detail of each of the claims presented before us is, for the reasons given, manifestly impracticable, we adopt the only course available to us, viz., to consider equitably the claims in the aggregate assigning to each its due weight according to our best judgment and making our recommendation in the form of special additional annual subsidies to the maritime provinces respectively as a final equitable settlement of the claims brought before us for adjudication. These additional annual subsidies so recommended are to be in substitution for the interim annual subsidies recommended by the Duncan commission. They should commence in the fiscal year 1935-6 and the interim annual subsidies recommended by the Duncan commission should cease at the end of the fiscal year 1934-5.
I draw hon. members' attention to the marked similarity with the present case. There you have interim payments under the Duncan commission, and here in this case you have transitional payments made under term 28.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE ADDITIONAL GRANTS TO NEWFOUNDLAND
speechtext: Those are subsidies. They are referred to as subsidies.

subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE ADDITIONAL GRANTS TO NEWFOUNDLAND
speechtext:
Not constitutional subsidies; that is the word the minister used. This commission was not set up pursuant to the constitution, as was the McNair commission, but was set up simply in the wisdom of the government of the day. It was a wise thing to do, but it was not a constitutional obligation. The minister by his intervention has very much weakened what little case he had. This was something that was done by the federal government in its wisdom in order to be equitable to the maritime provinces. It was not required under the constitution at all. I repeat:
They should commence in the fiscal year 1935-6 and the interim annual subsidies recommended by the Duncan commission should cease at the end of the fiscal year 1934-5.
The additional annual subsidies which we recommend are as follows:
To Nova Scotia, $1,300,000.
To New Brunswick, $900,000.
To Prince Edward Island, $250,000.
Now, what disposition was made of that? Sir George Perley was asked a question by Mr. McClure, who was at that time a member of this house representing a Prince Edward Island constituency, and Sir George Perley said that this recommendation would be dealt with either by a bill or by an item in the estimates. It appears in the Appropriation Act for one year only, for the fiscal year 1935-36. I have not examined the statutes for every year, but I am advised that it was dealt with in the same way every year until 1942, when it was embodied in a statute, chapter 14, entitled "An act to provide


for the payment of additional subsidies to the maritime provinces". It sets out these subsidies recommended by this report, and there is no time limit whatever put on them.
I do not think and I am not arguing that that is legislation in perpetuity. It is still on the statute books. They are still being paid in that form, and I take it they will go on being paid indefinitely. I would be very surprised if any government would ever reduce them, but circumstances might arise in the future when they would be increased. The minister was manifestly incorrect concerning a very important matter in his department with which he should have been better acquainted after two years at 18 hours a day.
If the government of Mr. Mackenzie King in 1942 could carry out what obviously was intended by the government of Mr. Bennett in 1935 in accepting the recommendation of the White commission and providing for additional subsidies to these three provinces and no others for an indefinite period, surely there is no reason on earth why the same action should not be taken in this bill except that this government wanted to punish Newfoundland, and for no other reason.
There could be no other reason except one. The year 1962 may be the end of the mandate of this parliament, and it may be that hon. gentlemen thought that by putting in that date it would give them an opportunity to make some more of those promises of which we had so many in 1957. There is no other explanation whatsoever that is credible to any dispassionate, objective person.
I suggest, sir, that hon. gentlemen-I will not ascribe motives-can take whichever explanation they like.
But this is not the only case. This morning I took a look at the Provincial Subsidies Act. These are not the constitutional subsidies of 1867; I understand those subsidies are provided under the Financial Administration Act at the present time. I looked into this matter. It is not very easy to trace the evolution of these statutes but these subsidies in the Provincial Subsidies Act are not the original constitutional subsidies; they are various other payments.
First of all there is one to New Brunswick, which is indefinite in time and is made on account of the repeal of duties on the export of lumber. It is not a very large amount, but it has been paid for a long time. It is $150,000 annually; there is no term on it; it does not end in 1962; it goes right on. It is not one of the constitutional subsidies at all; it is a payment that is made indefinitely, as this should have been.
There are at least eight or nine of those. Some of them are paid to Manitoba, several

to British Columbia and some to Prince Edward Island for various reasons, and they are being paid indefinitely. It does not necessarily mean that they are going to be paid forever, but they are being paid quite indefinitely. In other words the minister was completely and utterly wrong in his facts when he said that, apart from the constitutional subsidies, not one of the other nine provinces has anything anywhere that goes beyond March 31, 1962. It seems to me that this completely destroys any argument the minister might have had for putting this arbitrary date upon what was obviously intended to go on thereafter.
Now, for the benefit of the hon. and erudite member for Rosedale (Mr. Walker), I thought I would give him the definition of "thereafter" which can be found in the Concise Oxford dictionary. It means after that; in other words after March 31, 1962. This is the first definition.

speechtext: As a matter of fact, Mr. Chairman, my answer to this question is very simple. subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE ADDITIONAL GRANTS TO NEWFOUNDLAND
speechtext:
I am not agreeing or disagreeing with Mr. Smallwood. This was not my business. This was why the royal commission was appointed. I think Mr. Smallwood was understandably disappointed.
I said that the other day. If the hon. gentleman thinks he is going to get some satisfaction out of getting me to say that I disagree with Mr. Smallwood, well, he can get what satisfaction he likes. I have disagreed with Mr. Smallwood about a good many things and I expect to disagree with him about a good many more; but about this matter, Mr. Smallwood is the premier of Newfoundland and I am a member of this parliament, and I am taking my responsibility as a member of this parliament.
I have been very categorical about this and I will be so again. My view-and it is precisely the same view as the Leader of the Opposition has-is that if the government had carried out literally the recommendations of this royal commission they would have discharged the obligation under term 29, and they could not be criticized on the grounds of a breach or repudiation of the constitution at all.
I said the other day and I say again, like the Leader of the Opposition and like the premier of Newfoundland, that I think it would be much better to provide after a period for a review; and I think, like the Leader of the Opposition, that review should be a review agreed upon between the two parties to the original contract. But I say that this contractual obligation is very plain. It is to provide-I want to use the exact words-to provide the additional financial


assistance, if any, that may be required by the government of the province of Newfoundland to enable it to continue public services at the levels and standards reached subsequent to the date of union, without resorting to taxation more burdensome- perhaps I can just say more burdensome than the maritime average and save quoting the rather more precise words.

subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE ADDITIONAL GRANTS TO NEWFOUNDLAND
speechtext: To recommend, not to provide.

subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE ADDITIONAL GRANTS TO NEWFOUNDLAND
speechtext:
No, I am not talking about what obligation was on the commission. I am talking about what constitutional obligation is on this parliament. That is what the Newfoundlanders believed they were getting when they signed the terms of union, and that is what Mr. St. Laurent believed they were getting, too. That is perfectly plain if anyone will take the trouble to read Mr. St. Laurent's words a little earlier on in the same passage that has been read so many times before. He said, as found at page 289 of Hansard of February 7, 1949:
We on our side wanted to provide financial terms which would make it reasonably probable, if not certain, that the addition of Newfoundland to the economy of Canada would ultimately prove to be beneficial to both partners, to the older Canadians and to the newer arrivals. It was found, after more precise and careful study of the administrative problems that would be faced by the government of the province of Newfoundland, that the terms suggested in the offer submitted in October, 1947

Those were the terms referred to by the hon. member for St. John's West last night.
-would not be sufficient at the start to enable the provincial government to provide for its people on a basis comparable to that which is provided by the other Canadian provinces. It was felt there had to be quite substantial provisional grants, extending over a period of 12 years on a diminishing scale, to bridge the transition from the present economy of the island to the kind of economy which would make it possible for the provincial government to provide the people of Newfoundland with substantially the services that are provided for the rest of the Canadian people by their provincial governments, without resorting to a burden of taxation heavier, having regard to capacity to pay, than that which bears upon the people of the maritime region.
There is no doubt that is what Mr. St. Laurent indicated was the obligation, as between term 28 and term 29, that had been assumed in the terms of union. I am going to do something I do not do very often in the house, and I hope I will not do it very often in the future. I made a speech outside of the house the other day to the Canadian club in Winnipeg in which I said something about this very point. I am going to inflict it on

the committee because I think it is put more briefly here than I could put it if I ad libbed.
But the great snag in the negotiations was provincial finance.
I was talking about the negotiations with which, I will admit quite frankly to the hon. member for Rosedale, I was very closely associated although I was not a member of the negotiating team. I was in very close touch with them, as was natural because of the position I held at that time, in the prime minister's office.

speechtext: That is not what you said earlier.

I said I had nothing to do with the drafting of term 29, and it so happens I had nothing to do with it. I would not have been ashamed of it, if I had, but the truth happens to be that I did not. Since the question was raised I thought it might be just as well to dispose of it. That does not mean to say I did not have a good deal to do with these negotiations. I have never said I did not. I have never been ashamed of it. Indeed, there is nothing I am prouder of than any little part I had in helping to complete confederation.
But the great snag in the negotiations was provincial finance. How could enough revenue be ensured to the new provincial government to carry on the provincial administration on Canadian standards, without making provision for Newfoundland from the federal treasury on a scale which would seem unjust to all the other provinces?
That was the question; that was the problem.
I can well remember one evening when Mr. St. Laurent told me he was afraid that problem just could not be solved.

subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE ADDITIONAL GRANTS TO NEWFOUNDLAND
speechtext: Where was that?

subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE ADDITIONAL GRANTS TO NEWFOUNDLAND
speechtext:
It was in a private conversation I had with him at the end of one of the sessions of the two negotiating committees, when he was very discouraged indeed about the prospect of meeting this problem, which I admit at once is a very, very difficult problem indeed; as the royal commission showed, because of the great disparity between the development of the rest of Canada and the development that was possible in Newfoundland on account of some of the sad events to which the hon. member for St. John's West referred last night and with some of which he was rather intimately associated.
That problem was finally met by the recognition of a principle. In simple language that principle was that the new province should have eight years to build up its public services, and at the end of those eight years the province should be provided whatever additional financial assistance was needed to continue the public services of the province
Grants to Newfoundland without a higher level of provincial taxes in Newfoundland than in the maritime provinces. That principle was written into the Canadian constitution in term 29 of the terms of union. That is an obligation that the people of Newfoundland expect, and have a right to expect, the people of Canada to live up to.
That is the position I take. If I may say so, it is the position I have always taken on the matter, and as far as any overselling of it is concerned, I have never done anything except to point out, sometimes to people who did believe that it meant more, that all it meant was a guarantee of maintenance of the services as in 1957.
The hon. member for St. John's West tried to make a lot of that last night. He tried to make a lot of his statement that the Liberal opposition was trying to put services back to 1957. We are not trying to do anything of the kind. We are trying to get this right to which Newfoundland is entitled under the constitution, so that the money we get under the Atlantic provinces grants or anything else the government provides can be used in Newfoundland as in all other provinces to improve services. But the hon. member for St. John's West seems to want to force Newfoundland after 1962, because of the loss of these rights, to use money that other provinces can use for improvements for the purpose of continuing existing services. As precisely as I can put it, that is the difference between us.
While I am on my feet there is one other thing I should like to say, if I have not exceeded my time. Last night the Minister without Portfolio referred to the surpluses in Newfoundland and compared them with the colossal deficits of the Minister of Finance, I thought rather unkindly and rather to the minister's discomfort. The fact of the matter is, of course, that while Newfoundland has had a surplus on current account the hon. gentleman, as a former member of the house of assembly, knows very well that there is a very substantial deficit on capital account. He knows, I am sure, that because this government failed to act last September, when we pleaded with them to act, it has cost the government of Newfoundland over half a million dollars in interest payments, which money could have been used to much better advantage in that province if action, even the kind of limited, attenuated action being taken now, had been taken then.

Mr. Chairman, we have been listening for the last two days to this debate, which has reached bombastic proportions at times. I must frankly admit that when the debate started I was not too familiar with the circumstances surrounding this bill. At the conclusion of two days of debate on it I must admit that I am still confused on various points.
However, from sitting back and listening to both sides of this debate, I have reached a couple of conclusions. The first is that this is not by any yardstick the worst bill this government has brought into this house. In fact, as submitted by the Minister without Portfolio, there may even be the possibility that this bill will be a better one, or will bring more benefit to the province of Newfoundland than what it is enjoying at the present time.
I think the highly important factor here is that what they had before was something they had by right of confederation and that what they will have in the future, if we adopt this bill, is something they will have by right of the Conservative government. I wonder why this government should think Newfoundland or any other province should be beholden to them even though they do not want to be so beholden. It reminded me of a cartoon I saw in a newspaper not so long ago. I do not know what newspaper it was, and I do not know just what the subject was. However, it certainly was very appropriate at the time. It showed a baby sitting in a high chair with a very firm nurse, and there was no mistaking the features of the nurse. They were those of our Prime Minister. He held a bottle of medicine and a spoon and the caption was, "So you don't

like it; so it is good for you", I believe this bill would fit that particular cartoon very well.
The hon. member for Bonavista-Twil-lingate listed a couple of reasons which he believed were the only possible reason for this measure. However, I think he left out one possible reason, though I think he touched on it in his later remarks. I think that reason can be found if hon. members would look at page 1033 of Hansard for this session dealing with another matter, and that is the creeping paternalism of both the Prime Minister and the government he heads. In fact this bill says in as many words to the people of Newfoundland, "Never mind confederation. We can look after you better than anybody else, in fact better than you can look after yourselves".

On that point I should like to say that I agreed with the minister at the time. I had made an error and I admit that fact right away. It was March 31, 1961. I think I made it plain that I was conceding the minister's point, because I said to him right away, did he think that "thereafter $8 million per annum" means for one year only, because he has provided $8 million for one year only. The minister said these White subsidies had been "assimilated", which was his word, to the constitutional subsidies. I am glad they have been assimilated. I think they should have been. speechtext: In reply may I say this. My friend does not seem to be convinced. He speaks of the rule. It is a Pickersgillian rule. Nobody speaks as he did. Let me read from Hon. Mr. Lewis of the Newfoundland government.

according to the preamble, pursuant to the recommendations made by the royal commission. It is a rejection of the recommendations of the royal commission; it is a rejection of a most important part of those recommendations. The minister shakes his head. It is not difficult to prove that.
The hon. member for Rosedale spent a lot of time on this argument whether the royal commission's recommendations have to be accepted or rejected. There is no argument about that. The government is perfectly within its rights in rejecting this part of the recommendations of the royal commission, which I submit they do in this particular section. They can do that if they so desire. Quite apart from the moral obligation they may have to carry it out, they have no legal obligation to do so, and they do not do so in this particular section. In other words, it is a deviation from the recommendations in one respect, though the minister challenged us a few moments ago as to whether we would agree to a deviation in any other respect; that is, in respect of the amounts of the recommendations, as to that my hon. friend from Bonavista-Twillingate said he felt that the government would have been discharging the obligation that it had under the royal commission if it accepted the figures in that report. These figures are here but the last particular line of this section says: "fiscal year 1961-62, $8,000,000."
Mr. Chairman, that is no recommendation of any royal commission because the same section of the royal commission recommendation, section (e), on page 40 of their report, does not read "$8,000,000 for the fiscal year 1961-62", it says: "thereafter $8,000,000 per annum". But the way this appears in this particular section does indeed carry out the Prime Minister's wrong and misleading interpretation of these recommendations which he gave-and I have put this on the record already-at Saskatoon, and he has never denied it; he has never even tried to explain this remark which was so misleading. It was carried by the press all over Canada. He said that the recommendation to end in 1962 special payments to Newfoundland under article 29 of the agreement was made by a royal commission. It was made by no royal commission but it is certainly made in this particular bill. Perhaps that is why this section appears in this form. Perhaps it is because of the statement made by the Prime Minister at that time, and which he made in the House of Commons in substantially the same terms on March 25, and which

has already been quoted, and I think fairly, to the Prime Minister. The minister himself added another sentence or two but I think they were on the record earlier as well.
A great effort has been made-and it seems to me to be one of the most meaningless operations that could be performed in the House of Commons-to explain away the meaning of the word "thereafter". I do not propose to spend very much time on that. According to hon. gentlemen opposite "thereafter" has no meaning. It got into the report of the royal commission perhaps by a typist's error. It has no meaning at all; it has no significance because the only alternative to putting in the word "thereafter" was presumably perpetuity. That argument is so fallacious and so absurd and has been so completely dealt with that perhaps we need not waste any more time on it. The idea that the members of a royal commission as experienced, intelligent and qualified as these were, would put that word in without any understanding of its meaning at all is just too nonsensical to labour. The meaning is clear.
In their view it meant after that until a change was made by agreement $8 million a year should be paid to the government of Newfoundland. That constituted a floor, a security for Newfoundland in respect of this matter which was enshrined not only within the royal commission's recommendations but in term 29 because-and this is the core of the argument-there is an obligation in term 29 not merely to appoint a royal commission but there is an obligation on the federal government, on the federal parliament, to pay the amount which is required to ensure that the level of services do not fall below a certain point. That is the obligation.
When the royal commission put in these words "thereafter $8,000,000 a year" they were discharging an obligation to ensure that that amount at least would be allocated to Newfoundland until a change was made by agreement between Newfoundland and the federal government. By the removal of that word and by the removal of that concept they have removed the security that the people of Newfoundland felt they were getting under term 29. Perhaps the government in the future, perhaps parliament in the future will, as a result of a review, make available to Newfoundland far more money than $8 million a year, but there is no assurance. It has been taken out of a constitutional guarantee and it has been turned over to the good will of the federal government.
Perhaps in 1962 the good will of the federal government will be great, and perhaps it will make generous provision for Newfoundland in respect of services. I do not know;
Grants to Newfoundland but now the government and the people of Newfoundland have to depend on that good will which would be expressed presumably as a result of the review which will be undertaken. There is no incompatibility in the position that we have been taking on this side in regard to this matter, and the idea of a review. The two things are not incompatible. Of course, there can always be a review at any time, a review called by one party or the other. But pending that review and pending any decision made from any review, Newfoundland could, if the terms of the royal commission recommendations had been carried out, always count on this floor to ensure that the obligation of term 29 would be carried out, namely a level for its services.
That concept, that security, that floor, has been completely changed by this particular section of the bill. Mr. Chairman, I need hardly say, after what we have been saying in the committee and in the house, that this section is not, we think, satisfactory in any way, shape or form. In essence it means this. Without any provision for the future, after 1962, the people of Newfoundland are merely being told that big brother will look after them. subtopic: LEGISLATION TO PROVIDE FOR THE HUMANE SLAUGHTER OF FOOD ANIMALS
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill C-71, to provide for the humane slaughter of food animals.
He said: Mr. Speaker, as hon. members know, the matter of humane slaughter of food animals was the subject of quite exhaustive investigation during this session of parliament by the standing committee on agriculture and colonization. I am sure that all members of the house would wish to join with me in expressing appreciation to that committee and to the organizations and individuals who presented evidence to it.
The committee, in its report tabled on June 16th, recommended that parliament require the humane slaughter of meat animals in plants covered by the jurisdiction of the Meat Inspection Act. This bill gives effect to that recommendation. It will ensure that humane slaughter practices are followed in plants that are within the jurisdiction of parliament and come under federal meat inspection. These account for some 80 per cent of the total slaughter of meat animals.
The committee had recommended that this objective be achieved through an amendment to the Meat Inspection Act. On reflection, it was considered preferable to provide for it by a separate statute rather than as an amendment to the Meat Inspection Act. Hon. members will note, however, that the bill is tied closely to the Meat Inspection Act. It requires meat slaughtering establishments registered under that act to conform with the requirements of the regulations under this act. The act will be administered by officers now engaged in the administration of the Meat Inspection Act, and the bill clothes inspectors with the same powers as they possess under the Meat Inspection Act.
The committee report recommended that certain practices in association with the slaughter of meat animals be considered to be inhumane, and that certain other practices be considered to be humane. It will be noted that the bill does not list acceptable or unacceptable practices specifically, but provides for them to be established by regulation. This will permit the approval of slaughter methods and devices which have now

Humane Slaughter of Food Animals been determined to be humane and will provide the necessary flexibility to recognize others which may subsequently be developed.
The committee recommended that the operation of the proposed law be postponed for a reasonable time to enable all persons affected by it to take the necessary steps to comply with the law when it becomes effective. This will be dealt with by regulation, as the amount of time needed to enable the persons concerned to comply with humane slaughter requirements will vary with different classes of livestock. The packing industry has already adopted the use of mechanical stunners for cattle, as recommended by the committee, and there need be no delay in this respect.
Considerable study and experimentation has gone into the development of humane slaughter methods for hogs and other small livestock, and this has progressed to the point where adequate alternative methods for the humane slaughter of these animals should soon be available. While a reasonable period will have to be provided for the installation of the necessary facilities, I should like to assure the house that the minimum time possible will be allowed. I would certainly envisage that the regulations would be completely in force within a year.
As the house knows, the committee on agriculture and colonization considered whether the objective of humane slaughter should be achieved by way of an amendment to the Criminal Code or by a statute limiting its direct jurisdiction to establishments operating under federal meat inspection. As I noted at the outset, it recommended the latter procedure. The Criminal Code has, of course, for many years contained a provision requiring the humane treatment of animals. This will continue to apply.
There has been lacking, however, any special provision prescribing in detail the practices that may or may not be employed in the slaughter of meat animals. The bill now before the house and the regulations under it will establish those procedures in meat slaughter operations coming within the jurisdiction of parliament.

subtopic: LEGISLATION TO PROVIDE FOR THE HUMANE SLAUGHTER OF FOOD ANIMALS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the minister's statement was quite comprehensive but I wish that its substance had formed part of the bill. In looking at the measure it seems quite a simple bill but I should like to say that a measure of this kind can have far-reaching and serious effects. In fact, as hon. members know, anything that at any time may touch upon religious beliefs or religious practices is an extremely delicate matter. I should therefore like to ask for the patient and considerate indulgence of the house while I deal


with this matter because the bill itself could seriously affect the religious beliefs and practices of an important sector of Canadians.
I should like to say, Mr. Speaker, that certainly the principle of the bill is universally accepted and it is indeed a very laudable bill. But we must be careful that in doing one good thing we do not inadvertently do another thing that might destroy or interfere with other universally accepted principles. In this instance, Mr. Speaker, in legislating on methods for the humane slaughter of food animals, the house should be careful that we do not destroy or invade the freedom of religious practices of Canadians. I suggest that the house should seek a synthesis so that both principles can be preserved. It is to this objective that I want to address myself for a few moments.
Lest anything I might say should be interpreted as meaning that I do not support a measure of this kind, let me say at once- and make it as clear as language will permit -that I support any measure that will ensure humane treatment of animals. I do this not only out of personal conviction, but even more so because of the ethical and religious teachings which we receive from earliest childhood. The theory of kind treatment of animals is as old as the Jewish religion itself. It is first mentioned in the Ten Commandments. In the fourth commandment we are directed not to labour our animals on the Sabbath. It also directs that our animals be treated with the same kindness and the same consideration in that regard as even our own sons and daughters. That is indeed a far-reaching lesson on kindness to animals.
There are many other effective lessons on this point and I should like briefly to mention but a few. I do so, because I feel that the subject matter touching upon religious beliefs and practices is an extremely delicate one, as I said a moment ago. I should like to support that statement by saying that if a method is being used in the slaughter of animals for food purposes for people of the Jewish religion, it is not without careful consideration to kindness to animals.
For example, do hon. members know that no one practising my faith is permitted to sit down to a meal unless he first makes certain that his animals have been watered and fed? It is also forbidden to yoke a strong animal with a weaker one, lest there be suffering by the weaker animal. It is also forbidden to muzzle an ox when he treadeth the corn-and this is almost a verbatim quotation-because the ox should not suffer undue anguish from not being able to partake of the plenty around him. If he is muzzled he is not able to do so.

Another interesting point I should like to make is this. No animal may be slaughtered within the sight of another animal lest it be caused unnecessary anguish. Hunting, for example, is forbidden lest undue suffering be inflicted by wounding; and in order to discourage hunting, no animal killed at the hunt can be consumed by those who observe the tenets of their religion.
I want to make one or two more observations along the same line. It is expressly forbidden to ship over long distances or to keep in market places unweaned calves or kids lest they be deprived of food in that way and therefore suffer unduly. Judging from these humane religious teachings I venture to point out that I could be speaking for the oldest humane society in the world.
It may also be interesting for hon. members to know that according to a standard medieval ethical work-and I now refer to the Book of the Saints-we are told that a man will be called to account before the Judge of judges for any pain he has caused to an animal. But to bring this ancient record of kindness up to date may I say this. It is a fact that the founder of the royal society for the prevention of cruelty to animals was of the Jewish faith. Mr. Lewis Gompertz who was its first honorary secretary and, I believe the first president of the society for the prevention of cruelty to animals in the United States, was also of the same faith.
May I just touch on another point of interest. In the Jewish religion the taking of the life of an animal is not treated lightly. The slaying of animals for food is considered to be a religious rite and is accompanied by a prayer as a sacrifice. The act is performed by a religious functionary who must be a person of approved high moral character, specially trained and possessing a thorough knowledge of the precise rules and regulations to slaughter an animal without pain. He must be steady of hand, qualified by examination, certified and subjected to reexamination at frequent intervals by ecclesiastical authorities who alone can license a person to exercise the calling of slaying animals for food consumption by Jews.
I hope, Mr. Speaker, I have indicated to some degree the high regard which the people of our faith are taught to have for all animals and the particular attention given to animals slaughtered for food purposes. This matter is independently commented upon in an editorial of the Calgary Herald of December 26, 1956. I should now like to read this editorial to hon. members. It concerned a dispute in Calgary involving the society for the prevention of cruelty to animals and some threats which were presumed to have
Humane Slaughter of Food Animals been made to institute prosecutions for the slaughter of animals in what was considered to be an inhumane way. The heading of the article is "The S.P.C.A. Corrects a Bad Mistake" and it reads as follows:
The Calgary society for the prevention of cruelty to animals has reversed the stand taken by its president a few days ago against what he termed the "inhumane" methods of slaughtering cattle under the Jewish kosher rites.
While the details behind its decision to reverse itself are as yet unknown to the public, the society has been well advised in retracting its earlier threat to lay a charge under the Criminal Code of Canada against the Jewish slaughterhouses here.
Making its retraction, it has, we hope, nipped a particularly nasty and prejudiced publicity campaign against a community whose regard for the lives and the proper treatment of animals dates back to a point where it is almost lost in antiquity. Never, in the long history of the world, has any group of civilized people had a finer record of kindness to animals-a principle which forms an integral part of their ancient religious laws- than the Jews.
Any slaughtering of animals for human consumption is bound to be a revolting sight to the majority of people who, happily, have been able to divorce the slab of steak, or other animal foods, on their dinner plates from the actual process of slaughtering. And every method of slaughtering must necessarily involve some pain and suffering to the animal whether it is b,y a blow on the skull with a heavy sledgehammer, a slaughtering "gun" which fires a steel spike into the animal's brain, or under the age-old Jewish rites. The chief aim, then, must be handling the slaughtering in a way which will cause the least suffering to the animal, and there is in existence even when compared with the so-called modern methods an abundance of medical and other evidence that the Jewish procedure is as humane as any other, and perhaps less open to error or careless and faulty handling. Furthermore, it has long been a recognized fact that for the animal the cruellest part of the slaughtering is from the time it is first driven into the slaughtering house premises where it immediately senses what is in store for it from the smell of blood and other odours unavoidably associated with slaughtering.
The ancient laws of Judaism were expressly designed to avoid unnecessary cruelty to the animals, under the pain of the lash and other severe penalties. And investigations from time to time-the latest having been by a commission of the British House of Lords within the last ten years have failed to uncover any evidence that the immediate and guaranteed method of completely severing an animal's jugular vein is not an acceptable means of ensuring a quick and merciful death.
By launching such a prejudiced campaign against the Jewish race and religion the SPCA has done a serious disservice to the Jewish people and to its own cause.
Unfortunately, however, Mr. Speaker, in spite of this long record, historic and religious, where we were taught to prevent unkindness or cruelty to animals, which I have just recited and which has just been confirmed by a quite independent non-Jewish authority, I would like to say that there is a sorrowful history revealed behind similar legislation in other countries which has affected the right of Jews to slaughter their

Humane Slaughter of Food Animals food animals according to their religious ritual. Most hon. members may not be familiar with this type of innocuous-sounding legislation.
During my own lifetime I have had occasion to be saddened by legislation which sprang from and followed from so-called humane slaughtering regulations. I do not in the slightest, Mr. Speaker, impute any such motives to the sponsor of this bill. I attribute to him only the loftiest consideration based purely on the humaneness of the procedure of slaughtering food animals. Unwittingly and unknowingly, however, many of these benevolent activities have in the past covered ulterior and malevolent desires. Humane slaughter legislation has been used as a springboard for devious antireligious campaigns, and in some countries ritual slaughter has been completely banned. The histories of those countries stand out as a blot on the escutcheon of modern civilization.
I would like to read a paragraph from the Toronto Globe and Mail for July 14 last, headed "Humane Killing Religious Threat, Rabbi Warns". The article says:
Approval of a measure requiring the humane slaughter of livestock in New Jersey could be the first step in depriving Jews of their religious freedom, a Rabbi warned today.
Rabbi Pichas Teitz, leader of the orthodox Jewish community of Elizabeth, made this assertion during a public hearing on a bill directing meat packers to use humane methods in killing livestock.
He said a study of Jewish history shows Jewish sufferings began with approval of humane slaughter laws. He said Adolph Hitler prefaced his killings of Jews in Poland with a humane slaughter act.
I am sure that hon. members can, therefore, readily understand and appreciate the very genuine and deep-rooted concern, and even suspicion, which the 250,000 Jews living in Canada have about legislation of this kind. The Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) and his government inadvertently and very innocently may be made the victims of people with ulterior motives. I therefore feel it is my duty to call on them to exercise the greatest caution to make certain that if there are any diabolic or unrecognizable objectives which a measure of this kind may be loaded with, they should do nothing that may to the slightest degree invade the religious observances of our Jewish fellow Canadians, and do everything possible to adopt this legislation and also to safeguard their religious rights.
I repeat again, let no one think for a moment that I oppose any measure that outlaws inhumane treatment of animals. What I do say is that in the process of adopting this legislation we should not invade or minimize the freedom of religion


in Canada. We should seek that synthesis that will safeguard both and that certainly will solve this problem as it has been solved in the United Kingdom, in Scotland, in Ireland and in a great many other countries, and as it is now being dealt with in the United States itself.
I know that to find that synthesis is the objective of every hon. member of this house, and it is to this that I would now like to speak with respect to the bill itself. I have the fullest confidence that every hon. member who sat on the committee, as well as every hon. member in the house, has all the sympathy in the world and will do everything possible not to invade the religious rights of a large sector of Canadians. We find that the bill is entitled "An Act to Provide for the Humane Slaughter of Food Animals". But sadly enough, nowhere in the bill is humane slaughter of food animals defined. I think it is a mistake not to have in the bill a full and comprehensive definition of what is a humane method of slaughter and what is not a humane method of slaughter. The bill is so simple that to me it forebodes some danger. The most significant clause in the bill is the power that is given to the governor in council. I think parliament should know what is a humane method and what is not a humane method. We should define it and not leave it to the governor in council to decide.
Parliament appointed a committee and the minister referred very clearly to that committee. The committee made recommendations to parliament, and may I point out to the minister that when the Prime Minister introduced this measure for first reading on Friday -and he did this somewhat hastily, because he had to ask the unanimous consent of the house before doing so-he stated, and I quote:
This matter is one that has received the consideration of a committee, and the bill to be submitted I believe embodies the general recommendations made as a result of the deliberations of that committee.
Peculiarly enough, there is not a single word in the bill to justify that statement by the Prime Minister that the general recommendations of the committee were embodied in the bill. There is not a word. Not a single recommendation of that committee is embodied in this bill. To prove my contention, let me read a section of the report of the committee. I draw the attention of the minister especially to paragraph 7, which reads:
Your committee, after careful deliberation, submits the following recommendations for incorporation into legislation to provide for tile humane slaughter of food animals-
And the recommendations were, as this shows, expected to be incorporated into the legislation, because during its discussions the committee expressed some apprehension as to

whether or not this matter should be left to the governor in council or to officials no matter how able or how knowledgeable they might be, namely to decide for the committee, for parliament and for the country what is and what is not a humane method of slaughter. We expressly said that we wanted parliament to be able to decide that question, and we wanted it in the legislation. But, alas, not a single one of these recommendations is in this bill. For the benefit of any hon. members who are not familar with them, the recommendations were as follows:
(a)	That inadequate holding pens and/or unsafe ramps, inclines and floor surfaces over which animals must move in packing plants or slaughterhouses shall be considered inhumane.
(b)	That the combination of shackling and hoisting of a food animal before rendering it unconscious shall be considered inhumane;
(c)	Humane methods of slaughter shall be deemed to include
(i)	shooting,
(ii)	schechita (the Hebrew term for slaughter) as practised in compliance with Hebrew religious requirements;
(d)	Humane methods of pre-slaughter shall be deemed to include
(i)	stunning with a mechanical stunner,
(ii)	certain electrical stunning methods,
(iii)	the use of anaesthetising agents.
These recommendations are quite clear and we asked that they should be included in this bill so that we might be able to debate this subject adequately. We may now suspect that there may be other definitions made by order in council, and, unfortunately, we will not have an opportunity of debating them. I say, therefore, that I have the feeling that the Prime Minister possibly did not see the report of the committee, or that if he did see the report of the committee he apparently did not see the bill which, as I said, was rushed into the house last Friday for first reading. Being the busy man that he is, he probably took it for granted that the bill would follow the recommendations of the committee and my opinion is confirmed, apparently, by the right hon. gentleman's use of the words "I believe" in the course of his statement. If he had seen the bill the Prime Minister would not have used those words, because he would have been sure. I can readily understand that he might not have seen it because it might well have been handed to him hastily before he presented it for first reading. No criticism can be levelled at the Prime Minister for that, but I do address myself to the minister who is presenting this bill and I point out that the recommendations of the committee contained, as I said, a request that they be included in the legislation.
I hope the Prime Minister was shocked when he saw the contents of this rather controversial bill. Certainly I was shocked 66968-9-385
Humane Slaughter of Food Animals and no doubt other members of the committee who were responsible for the wording of the report as to the recommendations being included in the legislation were disappointed when they saw the bill. I would suggest to the minister that he should include in the bill itself what are considered to be humane methods of slaughter of animals for human food. That is the very purpose of this bill, and yet no single word is mentioned about it. If this were done, and if humane methods of slaughter were defined in the bill, it would certainly confirm by an act of parliament the recommendations made by the committee that humane methods of slaughter shall be deemed to include schechita, the Hebrew term for slaughter as practised in compliance with Hebrew religious requirements. If that were in the legislation it would be an attempt to synthesize the two good things we are attempting to do by this enactment, but having omitted to do that we have no such security.
May I call it six o'clock?

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. The amendment which I have just read was rejected by the government majority in the committee. I cannot understand why an amendment in those terms should have been rejected. Most surely it embodies a principle of which the entire house approves. Instead of leaving any doubt in the minds of the people of Canada that this measure might interfere with the religious rites or practices of anyone or might in any way invade those rights to the slightest degree I believe an amendment of this nature should have been adopted and incorporated in the legislation. Perhaps the minister will explain why such an amendment should not have won unanimous support. It merely states a principle which the house constantly approves. I know that the Prime Minister and members of the government acknowledge the freedom of religion and support and uphold that principle. Why, then, should the majority of the Prime Minister's party in the committee have rejected an amendment like that? I trust that the minister will explain because I feel that an explanation is owing.
In a further attempt to build up the synthesis about which I was speaking I introduced another amendment in the committee which I should now like to place on the record. I moved:
That the report be amended by adding thereto the following paragraph to be known as paragraph 8:
Your committee also notes that food animals killed in accordance with Hebrew religious requirements must not first be maimed or rendered unconscious by stunning or other means. We, therefore, further recommend that, before legislation dealing with this method is promulgated, further study be made of alternate procedures by which the animal can be delivered by humane means for the actual "shechita" cut. To this end your committee recommends that the government consult with leading Canadian packers and abattoirs with a view to the installation and use of casting pens or other procedures approved by government authorities, so as


to preserve for the people of the Hebrew and Mohammedan faiths the freedom of their respective religions and practices in Canada.
The purpose of that amendment was merely to ensure that we do not legislate in a way that would actually prevent the carrying out of the method of slaughter that is part of a religious rite. That, too, was rejected by the government majority in the committee which also puzzled me. The amendment simply sought to make certain that there would be no interference in the practice of the religious rites of any group through the fixing of a time limit.
As I examine the bill it appears to me to be designed to accomplish but one thing. It seeks to transfer to the governor in council the authority to declare what is and what is not a humane method of slaughter of animals. That, I believe, is what the committee sought to determine. The committee laboured for weeks, heard evidence, debated the matter in camera at several meetings and finally drew conclusions and reached decisions on the basis of the evidence presented to it. It determined what is and what is not humane slaughter. Are we to say now that the time of the committee was wasted? None of the findings of the committee are incorporated in this piece of legislation. We are removing from parliament the right of determination in this regard and placing it with the governor in council. This to me is the most poignant illustration of government by order in council.
But when parliament is in session, when parliament has appointed a committee to study a problem and the committee has sat and studied the problem and presented a report, the minister, or whoever it was that drafted this bill, is by no stretch of the imagination justified in ignoring that report completely and not bringing its recommendations before parliament. To say that these things will be decided by the governor in council is a derogation of power and authority. It is the business of parliament to decide these things. By the very nature of the bill parliament has not been asked to do that; parliament is deprived of that opportunity.
I presented that second amendment because I hoped that by that amendment the government might call in the abattoirs and the packers in Canada and consult with them. There was an area of a delicate problem there. While in principle we established that the Hebrew method, the Jewish method, of slaughter is humane, we might run into the danger that in the administration and in the regulations that will be laid down that lofty principle, that right which the committee has established, might be frustrated. There was the possibility of that being done.

Let me explain this to the house. While the schechita is declared humane, the committee found that the method by which the abattoir delivered the animals for the schechita cut was not considered humane. That is the section which speaks about shackling and hoisting being considered inhumane. Having outlawed the method of delivering the animal for the ritual cuts and stating legislatively that it is a humane method, and not making it possible really, as I said, could frustrate the intention of the legislation, I introduced that amendment and said: "Let the bill not come into force, let it not be promulgated until after consultation with the abattoirs, and until another more humane method of delivering the animal for the cut has been established". That, too, was rejected.
I say that the bold and the cruel effect of rejecting this amendment is a painful one because although the traditional Jewish method of slaughter may be declared humane, administratively it may be impossible to perform. I therefore respectfully say-and I repeat-that most certainly the measure requires the careful and conscientious consideration of the house. Because there might be frustration in the carrying out of the slaughtering in a way that will invade religious rights, religious freedoms, I urge respectfully on the Prime Minister who is a man, I know, of deep religious principles, who will not permit anything to be done that will invade the religious right of any ethnic group in Canada, since that certainly would be inconsistent with one of the principal principles urged in his bill of rights, to use his good offices to set out in this bill in language that the whole country may see and recognize as a law which safeguards the religious freedom of all people in Canada.
Moreover, Mr. Speaker, it should also be made clear by setting out these recommendations in the bill that this is not a measure which will remove from parliament the right of seeing and debating the real issues instead of delegating them outside of parliament.
The making of Canada's laws is the responsibility of parliament alone. Mr. Speaker, in order to bring before parliament the basic issues in this bill, I want to move an amendment, but I say to the minister at once that if he will declare that appropriate amendments along the lines suggested, or along the lines indicated and recommended by the committee, will be favourably considered by him I will withdraw my amendment. It may even be the wiser course, perhaps, to reconsider the bill altogether. Therefore, I would like to move the following amendment, seconded by the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Mcllraith):

Mr. Speaker, for two years now we have laboured over the question of humane slaughter. Originally it was the intention to introduce an amendment to the Criminal Code but it was thought that such an amendment would be too harsh under all the circumstances. So the standing committee on agriculture met over a period of six weeks during this session and after ten long meetings brought in a report which was tabled in the house. Before arriving at this report the committee on agriculture, under the able chairmanship of the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Stanton), heard evidence from all interested parties. Anyone who wanted to say anything was invited to say it. Free scope was given to all. We had three very distinguished members from the Canadian Jewish congress and

Humane Slaughter of Food Animals we benefited greatly from their evidence. We had representatives from the meat packers' council, the humane society and the society for the prevention of cruelty to animals. We had representatives from the Canadian Federation of Agriculture as well as experts and veterinarians who were authorities on the subject of humane killing.
I am very pleased that we now have before the house Bill No. C-71, an act to provide for the humane slaughter of animals. It is quite true that the bill is enabling legislation so that regulations can be promulgated by the Department of Agriculture, regulations which will be enforced by the inspectors under the Meat Inspection Act, regulations which will be drafted within the recommendations of the committee's report. I might also add, lest anyone feel that there is any usurpation of the powers of parliament, that these regulations must be advertised in the Canada Gazette and must be available to the house. If any hon. member should feel, once the regulations are tabled in the house, that they are not within the purview of the report or in any way infringe what he feels to be the rights of any such party, such honourable member can criticize any of the regulations in the house and has ample opportunity to do so either in the debate on the speech from the throne or when the minister's estimates are brought before the house.
The bill is short, simple and very much to the point. I want to thank the hon. member for Cartier (Mr. Crestohl) for agreeing with the principle of the bill which he states is universally accepted. I might point out to hon. members that the bill does exactly what the committee has recommended in paragraph six of its report, which paragraph reads as follows:
Your committee recommends, after due deliberation. that legislation amending the Meat Inspection Act be introduced to provide for humane handling and slaughter regulations.
That is exactly what the bill purports to do. There is nothing here that cannot be interpreted simply. Clause 4 of the bill states:
The governor in council may, for the purpose of ensuring humane slaughter of food animals in an establishment, make regulations respecting the manner of, and methods and devices to be employed in, the slaughter of food animals in an establishment.
I should like to point out that the report of the committee, which is very succinct, definite and to the point, is an excellent guide to the Department of Agriculture in drafting regulations. One might say, as I believe the hon. member who last spoke suggested, why should the regulations not be


incorporated in the bill itself? That might create a sorry plight, Mr. Speaker, in the event that any of the regulations turned out to be unjust or unworkable. It would then be necessary to wait until the next session of parliament to amend the regulations. After all, the regulations are subject to change from time to time but the one important thing is that they should be in keeping with and within the purview of the recommendations made by the standing committee on agriculture. So Mr. Speaker, I have a great deal of pleasure in supporting Bill No. C-71.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Cartier (Mr. Crestohl) has said that we on this side will support the principle of this bill. Because it deals with humane slaughter, I do not see how anyone could oppose such a principle; certainly not myself, who once had the privilege of working in a packinghouse in Chicago, during which I think perhaps I suffered as much as the animals did. The hon. member for Rosedale (Mr. Walker) has said that this bill is succinct, definite and to the point. It is certainly succinct and it is certainly definite. Whether it is to the point or not I am not so sure. He also said it was an excellent guide to the government, but I fail to see where the government in its wisdom in the promulgation of its orders will get very much guidance from it.
What this bill does, of course, is to give the government the authority under legislation to pass orders in council for the purpose of ensuring humane slaughter of food animals in an establishment, and make regulations respecting the manner of and methods and devices to be employed in the slaughter of food animals in an establishment. In other words, for this particular purpose it authorizes government to act by order in council. Some of us on this side, who in days past used to hear such violent talk of government by order in council, are naturally surprised that the government in a matter of this importance should have adopted this course.
The hon. member for Rosedale said, of course, "Well, the orders in council and the regulations will be tabled. The members can talk about them and complain about them in the speech from the throne debate and on the estimates, if they so desire." But that certainly does not meet the point, Mr. Speaker. So this bill provides government by order in council in this matter, and it is all the more surprising because, as the hon. member for Rosedale said, the committee laboured, and I am sure it did labour, for two years in dealing with this subject. That committee did not produce anything which

would justify this kind of limited bill. That committee reported as follows:
-after careful deliberation, submits the following recommendations for incorporation into legislation to provide for the humane slaughter of food animals,-
Not one of those recommendations is incorporated in this bill. So where is the guidance that is to be given to the government in this bill in the promulgation of its regulations? I am at a loss to understand why, if the committee laboured so long and so widely on this matter and produced recommendations, which were adopted, the government did not see fit at least to consider including some of those recommendations in the bill. If they decided that that was not desirable, surely, when parliament is giving the government power by order in council to act in this way to deal with humane slaughter, there should have been a definition of humane slaughter in the bill. The government is being given power by order in council to deal with humane slaughter when humane slaughter is not even defined in the bill.
Therefore, this bill is, we think, inadequate to accomplish the purpose which we all have in mind. While, of course, we support the principle of the bill, when we go into committee we will do our best to add to this bill provisions which will make it far more effective for that purpose than it is certainly at the present time.

Mr. Speaker, I just want to say a word or two on this bill. First of all, I would like to commend the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton), the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Harkness) and the agriculture committee for finding a way of legislating on this very difficult subject of humane slaughter of food animals. Ever since coming to the house, and I consider myself a veteran now, I have concerned myself over this very complicated subject. I have concerned myself first because it was something that I believed in personally, and also because I have had literally hundreds of letters from my constituents asking me to speak for them in the House of Commons on this subject.
The same request was put to the previous government, and I think actually it was my first question in the House of Commons. I asked the then minister of justice if he was going to bring in any legislation on this subject. This criticism by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) rather surprises me. He does not think that the bill spells things out enough, yet the previous government sidestepped it every time it was brought up to them because they said it was impossible to bring in such legislation.
Humane Slaughter of Food Animals
As the hon. member for York-Scarborough (Mr. McGee) has said, when the present government took office a group of us, mostly from Toronto but some from Vancouver, formed ourselves into a self-appointed committee to study the various ways of humane slaughter and bring suggestions before the Minister of Justice. We discovered, as the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton) had already discovered, that the drawing up of this legislation is a very difficult process. We discovered that some slaughtering devices did harm to meat, while others are so costly as to be almost prohibitive of purchase by the small packing firms. There were other difficulties. One was to find a practical and forceful way of legislating with regard to small slaughtering houses. As the Minister of Justice has said, it is just not good sense to enact legislation which cannot be enforced or which will not receive general public approval.
By the time I came into parliament, public opinion in connection with this matter was definitely aroused and in this regard I should like to pay tribute to the Toronto humane society and also to the Vancouver humane slaughter association. The Toronto humane society took up this question as early as 1948 and they claimed at that time that their main obstacle was the apathy, indifference and even the hostility of the general public. Due, I think, to the crusade conducted by the society, that apathy has now disappeared; it is a thing of the past. As a people we have a great regard for animals and I know this applied to many of our forefathers in Britain, and I think that when the situation was brought to the attention of Canadians they did feel aroused. A letter from the humane slaughter association of British Columbia pointed out that with the passage of legislation in the United States Canada became one of the very few civilized countries which had failed to provide protection for animals slaughtered for food.
There is wide unanimity that such protection is needed and that legislation of this kind had to be brought in. The problem which faced the Minister of Justice and the Minister of Agriculture was not whether or not to bring in this legislation but how to enforce it and how to prepare it in such a way that it was enforceable. Canadian packinghouses were agreeable to the legislation. In fact, one of them, Canada Packers in Toronto, has already put carbon dioxide equipment into all its plants at a cost of almost $250,000. The packinghouse workers union was also in full agreement, and gave its full support to humane slaughter and, certainly, I feel the general public will welcome this legislation and the enactment of Bill No. C-71.
