I pointed out at that time, as the previous speaker has just done, that Canada was one of the few countries left in the civilized world which had not produced some type of legislation to deal with this matter.
There is, I believe, unanimity of opinion with regard to the necessity of legislating for humane slaughter of food animals, and without going into details at this stage, may I say I think this legislation will be one more of those progressive steps that this parliament has taken, and I believe that in the end it will work out to everybody's satisfaction.

speechtext:
When the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton) referred this subject of humane slaughter to the committee on agriculture and colonization he asked me to take all the time that was necessary to procure whatever information and evidence that could be procured concerning the humane slaughter of animals. This the committee did, and the report which has been presented to the house makes it clear that dozens of witnesses were brought in from across Canada to give evidence before the committee.
These witnesses were called and, as the hon. member for Rosedale (Mr. Walker) has stated, as soon as the people of this country were aware of the fact that the subject of humane slaughter had been placed before the agriculture committee hundreds of letters flowed in from organizations, municipal councillors and individuals across Canada from the Atlantic to the Pacific. This illustrates the degree of interest which was taken in the subject.


After listening to the evidence which was presented, it was the considered opinion of the committee that schechita, or the Hebrew method of slaughter, was perfectly humane. Not only that, but it was considered it should come under the jurisdiction of the meat inspection branch and not under the Criminal Code, because members of the committee realized that if it were to come under the Criminal Code it could not be supervised effectively and the act could not be implemented as efficiently as it could if the responsibility were given to the meat inspection branch.
I might add that from the evidence given by the packinghouses and others it appeared that 80 per cent of the slaughtering across Canada would come under the jurisdiction of the meat inspection branch and that the other 20 per cent would come under the Criminal Code. Members of the humane societies are taking the responsibility of seeing to it that as far as possible any slaughtering which does not come under the meat inspection branch will be carried on in as humane a manner as possible.
I believe this bill is one that interests every individual across this country. I also believe the bill will meet the requests of those who have sponsored the cause of more humane slaughter of animals. It is my opinion that had some of the recommendations contained in the report of the committee presented to the house been spelled out specifically in this measure it would not have served a good cause. This bill is something new. We have not had legislation like it before. It may have been that had we spelled out a method of humane slaughter of animals in this measure, six months from now another way would have been discovered that would be far superior and with it spelled out specifically in the bill it would have been necessary to carry on the former way of slaughter until the next session of parliament when the legislation could be amended.
I think perhaps the hon. member for Cartier (Mr. Crestohl) is a little too suspicious. As I sat here this evening and listened to his remarks I concluded that he was taking the same position as had been taken by many hon. members on the opposition side from Newfoundland during the discussion of the bill concerning Newfoundland grants. They were suspicious of the government and it occurred to me that the hon. member for Cartier is also suspicious of the government and the Department of Agriculture. I assure the hon. gentleman that this government has the confidence of the people. I believe it was last Friday that the

Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) said that the regulations would conform with recommendations of the committee as presented to this house. I can say to the hon. member for Cartier that I am satisfied that those regulations will conform to the recommendations of the committee.
My remarks are few because it has always been my considered opinion that one should not spend 35 minutes building up to what he could have said within the space of five minutes. That has been the way hon. members of this house, especially those on the opposition side, have conducted themselves during this session of parliament in that they have spent many hours of time in needless discussion. A great saving in time could have been made if they had come down to brass tacks and said right off the bat what they intended to say.
This bill will serve a good purpose. It is something for which the people have been asking for many years. This government is to be congratulated for having brought this bill before the house in this session.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I promise the house I will not answer the general remarks of the last speaker about the conduct of the opposition during this session of parliament. I do not know that this subject is germane to the bill now before us but in any event I can assure him a very effective answer could be given on that subject. I do not want the hon. gentleman to assume from my silence that I do not think such an answer could be given.
It has been assumed by hon. members who have been speaking on second reading that the principle of this bill is to provide for the humane slaughter of food animals. The bill is entitled "An Act to Provide for the Humane Slaughter of Food Animals" and the first clause of the bill reads:
This act may be cited as the Humane Slaughter of Food Aniqaals Act.
It is quite obvious that the purpose of the bill is to provide for the humane slaughter of food animals but it is interesting that when you seek to find the principle of the bill by the ordinary method of reading it you find nothing at all about the humane slaughter of food animals. Clause 1 gives the name of the bill. Clause 2 gives a number of definitions. Clause 3 provides for the prohibition on people exporting meat out of a province or out of Canada unless slaughtered in certain plants. Clause 4 gives arbitrary power to the governor in council to make regulations. Clause 5 deals with some penalties for people who break those regulations. Clause 6 deals with some powers of inspectors. The principle of
Humane Slaughter of Food Animals the measure is not discernible from a reading of the bill. However, I assume that the principle is to provide for the humane slaughter of food animals and on that assumption I welcome and support the bill as I believe do hon. members in all quarters of the house.
The first problem the committee had to deal with was what method of legislating should be adopted. There were two methods possible. One was by further amending the Criminal Code which already contains one clause somewhat related to the subject. The other method was by legislating so as to control the operation within the slaughtering establishments over which the federal parliament has jurisdiction. It has to be borne in mind that ordinarily the slaughtering of animals would be a matter of provincial jurisdiction and the only method by which the federal parliament has jurisdiction is by controlling the establishments in which the slaughtering of animals which go into trade between the provinces or out of the country is carried out.
It was quite clear in the committee that such establishments handle something over 80 per cent of all food animals slaughtered in Canada. There are several reasons why I believe that the appropriate method to adopt was by dealing with this subject outside of the Criminal Code. I do not think I need elaborate on that point and I believe the committee was unanimous on it.
The best method is by controlling these establishments. I believe that we should not interfere with matters which are within the jurisdiction of the provinces. While I regret that it is not possible to provide proper legislation that would cover 100 per cent of the animals slaughtered, I believe the same results will in the end be accomplished by providing legislation governing the methods of slaughter used in the plants under federal regulation. I think the committee's recommendation on that point has been accepted. While it is true that technically we are not legislating by way of amendment to the Meat Inspection Act, certainly this bill is so closely related to it that no one could take objection on that point. It is so integrated with the Meat Inspection Act there could be no objection whatever on that point.
I believe the method of approaching the problem by a means other than amending the Criminal Code is the correct method in all the circumstances and I hope that as time goes on the provinces will bring forward appropriate legislation governing the plants that operate under their jurisdiction.
I am very much concerned with two main points in this legislation. Perhaps, in order

Humane Slaughter oj Food Animals to make myself clear on these two points, I should deal with the committee report which was presented to this house and which appeared in Votes and Proceedings of June 16. The first paragraph of the report deals with the reference; the second paragraph deals with the list of witnesses heard and it is indeed a very imposing list. The third paragraph deals merely with the evidence that the committee heard. The fourth paragraph deals with the submissions of suggestions made with respect to the methods of dealing with legislation on this subject. The fifth paragraph of the report notes that federal legislation under the Meat Inspection Act covers government inspected plants which perform approximately 80 per cent of the slaughtering of food animals in Canada. The sixth paragraph recommends this method of legislation on the subject. I want to draw the attention of the house to the seventh paragraph. It goes on to say:
Your committee, after careful deliberation submits the following recommendations for incorporation into legislation to provide for the humane slaughter of food animals.
Then follows several subparagraphs to that seventh paragraph: (a) dealing with certain conditions in the plants; (b) with certain practices in handling the animals immediate to preslaughter; (c) dealing with certain things that should be considered humane methods of slaughter and included in that, incidentally, is the finding that the schechita, or the Hebrew method of slaughter, is humane. Then (d) deals with humane methods of preslaughter. Paragraph 8 suggests that the operation of the proposed law be postponed to give the persons affected the opportunity to equip themselves to carry out the legislation. I think the minister dealt with this last point in his opening remarks.
The points I wish to make are these. First of all, I regret very much that the bill does not define humane slaughter. We are supposed to be legislating to provide for humane slaughter of food animals, but in the bill we say nothing at all about what humane slaughter is or is not. There are two or three ways of defining humane slaughter. One is by a list including methods of slaughtering that are humane and excluding other methods that are not. There is no declaration or definition in the bill of what constitutes humane slaughter at all and in my judgment that is a defect in the bill. Indeed, on that point, the house is asked to turn over to the governor in council, if the purpose of the act is to be accomplished at all, the right to determine what is humane slaughter.
It is perfectly obvious that there must be regulations to provide what devices shall be used and shall not be used, and certain details


of handling and equipment; but surely parliament ought in the legislation to declare or provide what is humane slaughter. Reference was made by the hon. member for York-Humber (Miss Aitken) to the legislation that was passed by the United States last year. I am very much interested to know that in the second section of that bill this very point is dealt with. In the first section there is a somewhat general reference, something analogous to what we would call a preamble, and the very first matter of substance dealt with is the point as to what is humane and what is not humane, the very thing that this legislation does not do. I am very critical of the government on this point because our legislation is defective in that it fails to do that. Then, there is the other objection to the failure to do that. We are turning over to the governor in council the right to do that, something that surely is the responsibility of parliament and properly belongs to parliament.
Finally, without extending the argument, I was most disappointed to hear my colleague, the hon. member for Rosedale (Mr. Walker), use the argument he did about arbitrary powers by regulation. Surely that is not an answer to the point at all. Surely on matters of principle parliament should be the one to legislate. It is not good enough merely to say that an hon. member can mention the subject at some time in subsequent years in a general debate. That is not a good enough answer. This giving of arbitrary power is a wrong principle; it is quite unnecessary here in this aspect of this legislation and it is not to be defended.
I wish the minister would deal with the point because, so far as I am aware, all other legislation on the subject has dealt with that point. I could be wrong on that. Undoubtedly the minister has studied more extensively the subject than I have but certainly the United States does provide for it in the bill itself, and certainly it ought to be provided for here. I am aware of no practical reason why it is not provided for in this bill and indeed, particularly in view of the fact that the committee which I think I can can say fairly was remarkably objective in its work-I think that is a proper reference to my colleagues of the committee-did try to work out something that would be satisfactory and did definitely recommend for incorporation in the legislation certain matters that involved definition of humane slaughter.
I am a little mystified as to why the minister and the government did not follow the recommendations of the committee. I am rather of the impression that the government as a whole is of the opinion that in this

legislation it followed the recommendations of the committee. I am reinforced in that view by the remark made by the house leader when he was indicating the legislation the other night when he said so in so many words, and by a reference made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) when the bill was given first reading. I think they indicated quite clearly that the government was of the opinion that the bill did follow the recommendations of the committee. I regret very much that it does not.
The second point I want to make reference to with respect to this bill is that Canadians generally, and I think properly so, have taken pride in the fact that Canadians as a whole have attained and preserved in this country a very high degree of religious freedom. I think all Canadians, and all members of parliament on both sides of the house, hold that view. The slaughter of food animals is a religious ritual with certain religious groups. In this bill now before us we have not put in any provision to protect that principle that I think all hon. members of the house assert. It just is not in the bill but instead the bill as submitted authorizes the governor in council to make regulations which could-and I do not for a minute suggest that the governor in council would do it-and are capable of taking away the religous freedom of religious groups in our country.
That is something that I do not think hon. members wish to do. I am somewhat at a loss to understand why that principle was not protected in the bill submitted to the house. I take the strongest possible objection to the omission from the bill of these two very important matters if the bill is to have any purpose or meaning at all. The first is the failure to define humane slaughter by some method, and there are two or three methods that can be used. The second is the fact that the bill provides in its present form for the governor in council to make regulations which might take away the religious freedom of whole religious groups. There is no protection for them at all in the bill. I do not see why that was done, particularly in view of the finding in the committee report that schechita is humane.
In view of that finding in the report, and I believe the committee was unanimous on the point, it is my view that the government may be stumbling into doing something they did not intend to do by reason of their failure to adopt any definition of humane slaughter. They may have inadvertently stumbled into doing something that I really think they did not intend to do at all in the drafting of this legislation. I should like to ask the minister to consider these two points and
Humane Slaughter of Food Animals to insert into the bill at the committee stage provisions that will cover them because I feel they are very important.
I will give the government credit. I very often hit them hard but I will give them credit for not having improper motives. I think their motives were probably of the very best and that it is a matter of inadvertence in the drafting. There may be some other reason but I am inclined to think that it was a case of inadvertence in the drafting and not appreciating these points. At least I am charitable enough to hope that was the case and to hope that they will be taken care of at the committee stage. If I interpret the principle of the bill correctly, as being to provide for the humane slaughter of food animals, I am certainly in accord with its purpose.

Mr. Speaker, I think most members of the house will agree-certainly I have never had any other idea in my mind-that the bill is a thoroughly non-partisan measure. As a


matter of fact, the speeches which have been made from both sides of the house have indicated agreement with the principle of the bill and with the idea that there should be some legislation respecting humane slaughter. Therefore I think that demonstrates the fact that the bill is not a party matter in any way. It is a government bill because it is the responsibility of the government to deal with matters of this kind. Therefore I was somewhat sorry, shall I say, that the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) and other members of the Liberal party should introduce a partisan attitude in connection with the bill and start making accusations that the government was taking arbitrary power, that the government was attempting to rule by order in council under the provisions of the bill, and things of that sort.
As I see the bill, I have always considered it-and I think most other people have done the same-as an entirely non-partisan matter. Certainly there is no idea in any way to take arbitrary powers or to attempt to rule by order in council through this bill. The only criticisms there seem to be over the bill are two in number. One is that the bill should be in a somewhat different form from that in which it is. The Leader of the Opposition, 1 think it was, said that this is government by order in council and the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Mcllraith) said that this was arbitrary power being exercised and so on. As a matter of fact, I think everybody who has ever had anything to do with the matter of providing legislation to deal with humane slaughter recognizes the fact that it is an extremely difficult matter to deal with. I imagine that the reason that the previous government never got around to introducing a bill to deal with this matter was the very fact of the difficulties that it presented, including difficulties of definition, difficulties as to the way in which to do it, and in fact difficulties of all kinds.
We have been attempting to bring in a bill providing for humane slaughter since we first came into power some two years ago. Hon. members will perhaps recall that we introduced a bill in the first session in 1957. When it was introduced it was stated that it was introduced so that it could be studied and so that people concerned with and interested in the matter could make representations as to whether they thought it was a reasonable bill and a proper way in which to deal with the matter. The same bill was reintroduced in the next session which was the session prior to this one. Then all kinds of objections came about it. That bill was in the form of an amendment to the

Criminal Code. It became quite apparent that there was no means at all of getting any sort of agreement on that particular bill or a bill like it. As a result of that discovery we sent this whole matter for study to the committee on agriculture and colonization. That committee studied the matter, as has been indicated, over a long period of time and with great care and they brought in certain recommendations. This bill is intended to carry into effect and it will carry into effect the recommendations of that committee.
The statement has been made many times today that it is not carrying into effect the recommendations of the committee. Everybody in this house knows that every bill dealing with matters that require any sort of detailed regulations have a provision that regulations may be made covering various points or covering the matter dealt with. Every bill has a provision of that sort. This particular bill provides that regulations may be made for the purpose of ensuring humane slaughtering of animals in establishments, regulations respecting the manner of slaughter and the methods and the devices to be employed in slaughtering food animals in establishments. I can assure the house now that the recommendations of the committee in connection with that matter and the opinions expressed in the committee will be followed out in as complete detail as possible in drawing up these regulations and ensuring that the findings of the committee or the opinions expressed by the committee are carried into effect.
The complaint was made by the hon. member for Ottawa West, the hon. member for Cartier (Mr. Crestohl), and I think the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson), although I am not sure of that, that in this act there is not a definition of humane slaughter. I have never yet seen a satisfactory definition of humane slaughter. Every definition which has been proposed has certainly met with considerable objection. It is a practical impossibility to give a definition of humane slaughter which you can put into legislative form in an act. The only practical way of dealing with that matter is to have a long list spelling out in detail the things which can be done and which are accepted as humane and the things which cannot be done and which are held to be inhumane. Things of that sort are things which can be covered in regulations. Those are things which regulations are meant to cover. They are not the sort of things which should fill up page after page of a bill of this kind. That is the reason why the bill is in this form.

Therefore the only slaughter not covered by this is slaughtering done on farms by farmers themselves, and in small slaughter-houses where they have just a local trade, and things along that line, and some which have a trade over a small area within a province and therefore do not come under the Meat Inspection Act. in European countries are humane and should be authorized or not. That is one of the reasons why we thought some of the methods used over there should not be specified.
As a matter of fact, although there are various methods which we do think are thoroughly humane at the present time, there is no doubt that many more will be added later. It may be that some of these might be considered, at some future time, not as humane as some others which develop. Therefore, in order to carry into effect and keep in effect a thoroughly humane system of slaughtering in this country, it is better not to have something bound down too firmly in the act. Subclause 2 deals with the nature of evidence. I speak of this matter because it concerns me not only as a member of the house but also as a lawyer. I

should like to ask the minister to explain this subclause which states as follows:
(2) In a prosecution for a violation of this act, it is sufficient proof of the offence to establish that it was committed by an employee or agent of the accused whether or not the employee or agent is identified or has been prosecuted for the offence.
I am concerned with the possibility of prosecuting someone and not identifying the person who committed the offence as being the agent of the man being prosecuted. Anyone can do something which is an offence under the act. It can be a passerby, a trespasser or a stranger who may commit an offence. It is found that an offence has been committed and then you proceed to prosecution. I think it is unfair to say that the man who committed the offence should not necessarily be identified as the agent of the accused. I think it is a fallacy in criminal law or criminal procedure not to be able to identify the man who committed the offence as being the agent of him whom you prosecute. I think that the theory of criminal law would certainly be exploded if that were made possible by any legislation of parliament.

subtopic: LEGISLATION TO PROVIDE FOR THE HUMANE SLAUGHTER OF FOOD ANIMALS
speechtext: This is the ordinary provision really, that the employer is responsible for the actions of his agent or employee in matters of this kind. You have the same sort of thing in the Seeds Act which we amended here a little while ago. The same question was raised in connection with the Seeds Act. The only difference here is whether or not the employee or agent is identified. That is the only difference here at all. The reason that is so is this, as these animals go along on the rail there may be two or three people at fault and it may be impossible to identify exactly which one was at fault. The fault may be shared among four or five. For example, an animal might not have been sufficiently stunned. The interval between the time it was stunned and the time it was bled and thus finally completely dead might be too long. Who is responsible? It is impossible to determine whether it was the man who did the stunning who was responsible or whether it was the man who was supposed to do the next operation; he let too long go by and so on. You might have a series of three or four things along that line and it is impossible to say that A, B, C or D was the one who was responsible. This provision is to make it possible to prosecute when you have what is definitely a contravention of the act without having to say, "John Jones was the man who was responsible for the contravention".

Mr. Chairman, when we were considering this item on June 25 I agreed to answer those who had spoken when we next were on the estimates, and I think perhaps I might do that right now. We had a useful contribution to the debate on the opening item by hon. members on the other side of the house, and they raised some questions which are worthy of comment.
The Leader of the Opposition dealt chiefly with recent trade developments with the proposed Atlantic free trade community, and he mentioned trade with Japan and discussed the subject of uranium. I pointed out in my earlier remarks that the annual report of the department had been enlarged on this occasion in its earlier part in order to deal somewhat more comprehensively with general
6092	HOUSE OF
Supply-Trade and Commerce trade policy and trade activities, and some of the problems that were raised have been covered fairly fully in the annual report. But in answer to the Leader of the Opposition I would say that we are following very carefully developments in Europe. We have a clear appreciation of their significance, not only for our exports but for world trade generally. In the sessions of GATT in 1957 and 1958, when I was present at the meetings, we made the point that we hoped the development of the common market in Europe would not be restrictive in its nature and that barriers would not be raised against trade. It is important to recall that the members of the six nations who comprise that common market in Europe are all members of GATT and have obligations under that international arrangement.
The Leader of the Opposition drew attention this year, as he did last year and on other occasions, to the need, as he put it, to work out some special form of North American association with the European economic grouping in order-I think this is what was in his mind-to avoid having the world get into the position where trading blocs are established with barriers raised among them, whereas the policy pursued by Canada over the years has been to promote multilateral trade. That policy is being pursued at the present time and our trade is extensive throughout the world with most countries of the world.
His suggestion, however, is certainly worthy of consideration because the closer are the economic ties between the North American continent and western Europe the better for us all because of our other arrangements with those countries within NATO. When Dr. Hallstein, the president of the European economic commission, was in Ottawa two or three weeks ago the Canadian point of view was presented to him and he showed his appreciation of that point of view, namely that barriers should not be raised against trade between our country and the countries of the common market.
On the subject of Japan, the Leader of the Opposition quite rightly stressed the importance of our trade with that country. It is a trade which has been developing over the years and we share his view completely. In the forum of GATT we have expressed our interest in giving Japan the full arrangements which are available under GATT and have urged that other countries do the same as we are doing. It is important that the economy of Japan be strengthened and we are co-operating closely with Japan toward that end. It is one of the major trading countries of the world today.


It is a country with whom we are developing quite a substantial trade, and we find that Japan is either second or third best customer for our Canadian wheat. The difficulties that we have been experiencing with Japan with some of her imports are being cleared away. Very useful discussions have been held with the Japanese looking toward a modification of their exports to this country, particularly in the field of textiles. Those conversations with the Japanese representatives have been, as I say, very useful, and I think results are being achieved.
I cannot deal at as great length as I might with all the matters raised in discussion with hon. members opposite, but I would like to discuss some of the problems raised by the hon. member for Ottawa West who has over the years been very much interested in Canada's trade. He asked several questions with regard to our trade with the West Indies, and of course last year in the house he raised this problem on another occasion when there was a rather extensive debate. The West Indies is an important area for Canadian trade and has been so for generations. We are attempting to maintain and strengthen our trade relations with the West Indies and from the experience I had there just over a year ago, visiting the West Indies, I received the impression that they were equally interested in enlarging their trade with Canada. It is an important market for us. In 1957, Canada provided about 10 per cent of the total imports of the West Indies and a much higher proportion of their purchases of certain individual products such as flour, potatoes, salt cod and pickled meats.
There has been some change in the pattern of trade with the West Indies of recent years. We have not increased our sale of fish and flour to the extent that we would like, but these products do not now represent as large a proportion of the import market as they did in the past. In machinery and equipment there has been a marked increase in the requirements of the West Indies. We find that our exports are generally competitive in the West Indies. In some products we have increased our share of the West Indian market and I mention specifically bacon and ham, leather, motor cars and clothing. The West Indies represents an important market for manufactured goods from Canada and there is scope for an expansion of Canadian sales in this field. Hon. members realize that there have been restrictions on West Indian trade because of balance of payments reasons but these restrictions are being relaxed and new opportunities are being opened up for Canadian exporters.

We had a visit last year from the minister of trade for Jamaica and I recall his remarks to Canadian businessmen urging them to be more active in visiting the West Indies and attempting to arrange business there. Last winter a strong contingent of Canadian businessmen did visit the West Indies and they explored the market for themselves. At the same time, under the auspices of the Canadian government, a Canadian trade fair was in operation, first at Kingston, Jamaica and subsequently at Port of Spain, Trinidad.
The West Indies is, of course, a competitive market and competition is felt from Britain, the United States and other countries. The hon. member for Ottawa West raised the question of our trade with the West Indies in its currency aspect. Last year at the commonwealth conference we had a discussion with the United Kingdom and the West Indian representatives on that very matter, and it was agreed, and I quote from the report of that conference:
That joint consideration be given to all matters designed to improve and strengthen existing trade ties and ensure the closest possible trading relationship between the West Indies and Canada.
The removal of restrictions which has been taking place in the United Kingdom and in various countries of the commonwealth has also been taking place in the West Indies, and there is a relaxation of the restriction of imports from dollar countries.
With regard to the trade agreement with the West Indies which the hon. member for Ottawa West also mentioned we recognize -and it was recognized by the conference at Montreal-that a revision of the existing trade agreeement of 1926 between Canada and the West Indies would be necessary but it is dependent upon the establishment of a customs union in the West Indies Federation. The preparatory work for that has been under way for some time, and if it is advanced sufficiently by the latter part of this year we expect to hold trade discussions then with representatives of the West Indies to consider whether or not the trade agreement of 1926 might be extended.
The hon. member also raised the question of capital development in the West Indies and wondered whether or not Canada is playing her part in that. Canadian investment in the West Indies at the end of 1957 amounted to $130 million, exclusive of banks and insurance companies. That is a marked increase as compared with the figure for 1951 when Canadian investments stood at only $25 million. So there has been a five-fold increase in that period. That compares with the United States investment in the West Indies of $235 million at the end of 1956, the latest figure I have available. Canadian
Supply-Trade and Commerce banks and insurance companies have been very active in the West Indies for years. Four Canadian banks have branches there and ten Canadian insurance companies are established. In addition, various Canadian companies are operating in the West Indies. Without making the list complete, I mention light and power companies, companies manufacturing food products, optical supplies and woollen textiles. There is also, of course, the activities of Aluminium Limited which has developed bauxite products and produces refined alumina for shipment to Canada. There are also stores, machine shops, coastal and river steamers and ships carrying the trade between Canada and the West Indies.
The hon. member for Ottawa West also dealt with our trade with Japan and indicated some concern about a drop in our export sales to Japan last year compared with 1957. There was a drop in our exports of barley but an increase in our wheat and flour exports which went up from $68.5 million in 1957 to $71 million in 1958. The drop in barley exports was due to the fact that there was a bumper rice crop in Japan, and barley in that country is a substitute food for rice, so the requirement was not as great. In the first five months of 1959, taking this as the period for which the latest figures are available, exports to Japan amounted to $44.9 million compared with $40.3 million for the same period in 1958. I have already mentioned our intention to develop as far as we can our trade with Japan.
There was some discussion with regard to our general trade, contributed to by the Leader of the Opposition and the hon. member for Ottawa West. They were dealing with one month whereas I had been dealing with the figures in my possession for the period of five months.
Of the first five months of the present year, only in January were Canada's exports to the United States lower than in the corresponding month of 1958. In each of the four succeeding months, that is, February, March, April and May, they were higher and in the five month period as a whole amounted to $1,186 million compared with $1,135 million in the same period of 1958, an increase of 4J per cent.
There was some criticism of my remark to the effect that the increase in Canada's imports had been shared by all the major trading areas and some questions were raised in regard to that. My reference to imports was based, not upon particular selected months but upon all months in the year to date for which figures were available; that is, January to April inclusive. The totals for this period show an increase in imports

Supply-Trade and Commerce from the United Kingdom, the commonwealth countries, the United States and all other countries considered together. Comparing imports for the first five months of 1959 with the corresponding period two years ago shows purchases from the United Kingdom up by 6 per cent and purchases from the United States down by 12 per cent. These figures indicate that the position of British relative to United States goods in the Canadian market remains substantially better than in the early part of 1957.
The hon. member for Ottawa West raised a number of questions concerning the exports of surplus farm products. This, if course, overlaps with the Department of Agriculture. I believe the hon. member was concerned as to whether the sale of some of these agricultural products abroad would interfere with our general trade picture. My understanding is that in all these sales care is taken so that there will be no interference with our trade in general and so there will be no accusation of practising anything in the way of an unfair method in trade. My colleague, the Minister of Agriculture, of course, could give a more specific answer in this regard.
In selling our surpluses in export markets every effort is made to ensure that these sales will not give rise to repercussions in our international trade relations with other countries. Before a surplus product is released for export at a subsidized price the country of destination is carefully screened to make certain that we are not causing undue hardship to other suppliers to that market. With this careful screening of exports and through consultation with other governments concerned we have, in the main, been able to export these products without creating serious problems in our commercial relations with other countries.
The hon. member for Ottawa West raised a question with regard to our trade with Italy. It is important to note that a year ago Italy was greatly affected by the world recession. Industrial production levelled off and total imports declined by about 14 per cent. Imports of agricultural products also ran at a lower rate due to substantial improvements in local production. This year developments are more encouraging. Italy's foreign exchange reserves are now at a record level and with the introduction of external convertibility the country is in a position to remove many restrictions on dollar goods. There are also signs of a definite upswing in the Italian economy. We are expecting an improvement in our export sales to Italy as the year progresses.
The hon. member for Fort William asked a question or two with regard to whether

or not we were making a study of international trade and what trips or trade missions were in contemplation by the department. We make a continuing and close study of international trade. Our trade commissioners are continually reporting to the home office. We have a very efficient trade commissioner service and we have an international branch which keeps closely in touch with all the aspects of international trade. We have an efficient service in so far as gaining information with regard to trade abroad is concerned and in passing that information on to our exporters here at home so that business opportunities are brought to the attention of Canadian businessmen. With regard to trade missions, I have nothing to announce at the moment. I believe the hon. member wanted to know about my own activities. I hope to visit some countries during the autumn months if it is at all possible but I am not in a position to indicate at the moment what visits I might undertake.

The hon. member for Vancouver East discussed the problem of the alleged control of United States firms over their subsidiaries in this country, and alleged restrictions in the trade of those subsidiaries. This information is requested in the questionnaire which must be completed before a company can be included in the department's confidential exporters' directory. Before we undertake assistance in promoting exports for the subsidiary of a foreign manufacturing company we have to seek an understanding, and readily obtain as a rule any needed assurance that the assistance which we extend will not be diverted to the benefit of production and employment in some other country, but only used for the benefit of Canadian industry.

Therefore, although the program may appear to be fairly large, the time available to the house is close to being that of a normal five days.

May I ask the hon. gentleman what is proposed by the government about the legislative items sent over from the Senate and announced tonight? Then, there is the bill of the Minister of Justice, and some amendments to another bill.

Mr. Speaker, it depends on the progress that we make with estimates. What I have announced here will carry over definitely for Thursday and Friday. If by tomorrow night we have made considerable progress and if by Friday we appear to be quite close to the end, then we will be able to determine when the legislation will be fitted in.
We can be sure that there will be no legislation tomorrow or Friday?
That is right, for Thursday and Friday no legislation.

It being 22 minutes past ten o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
